job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Zane Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did mechanical engineering at Nottingham and I've been a graduate engineer at a pump factory in Derby since October. I'm in a test bay for half the day, running pumps on a rig and writing down pressures by hand, and the other half I'm in the office updating drawings. I rent a room in a shared house with two lads from a call centre, and I eat my lunch with a fitter called Barry who's been at the factory since 1994.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the noise of the test bay and the smell of oil, honestly, and that you can see a pump pass or fail. What wears me out is the drive, forty minutes each way in a car that's older than I am. I owe about 19,000 and my mum slips me 50 quid now and then, which I hate taking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected. People have been shouting about computers taking jobs since my granddad's time, and he lived through factories being automated twice. I don't use any of these AI tools, so it makes no difference to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a bit relieved, because I'm not a computer person. I'd rather be in the test bay with a spanner than writing prompts. The thing on my mind is money, since my pay is okay but the car and the loan eat most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and try for the chartered engineer scheme next year. I'd look at a room closer to the factory so I'm not burning petrol, and I'd keep 100 a month for the loan. Nothing exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit stretched on money, but nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if the car broke down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to buy a cheaper one on finance, which I don't want, so I'd cut the gym and the takeaway first. And I'd ask Barry for a lift. He'd say yes and complain the whole way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Barry say about all this AI talk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lunch mate Barry says he's seen three of these, and the pumps still need testing. I think he's right, though he'd be the first to tell you he's never used a smartphone for anything but calls.

say: I'd say it's what I expected, because people have shouted about **computers taking jobs** for decades.
I don't use AI tools, so it **makes no difference** to me.
think: Privately I'm relieved, because I'd rather be in the **test bay** than writing prompts.
My real pressure is **money**: the car and the loan eat most of my pay.
do: Keep working and apply for the **chartered engineer** scheme next year.
Look for a room near the factory to cut **petrol costs**, and keep 100 a month for the loan.
feel: **Fine**, a bit stretched on money but nothing that costs sleep.
S0.quote: My lunch mate Barry says he's seen three of these, and the pumps still need testing.
fieldNote: He is calm about AI but **uneasy about money**; car and loan are the pressure, not technology.
His trust comes from **older colleagues** and his granddad's factory stories, not from research.
He is reluctant to take his mum's 50 pounds, a small pride point.

steps.text: Apply for the chartered engineer scheme next year
Look for a room near the Derby factory to cut petrol costs
Pay 100 a month towards the student loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds big, but I'd wait and see what it really does in a factory. In our office the drawing team is five people, and I could see software doing half of what they do. In the test bay, I can't see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd start to worry a bit. The office half of my day, drawings and checking, is the bit that goes, and then the company would want fewer engineers and more technicians. I'm slow with new technology and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stay as hands-on as I can. I'd ask to do more test work and commissioning, and I'd try to learn the new test-bay software when the company brings it in, because I wouldn't have a choice. Still, I'd not go on my own to use any AI tool; I'd wait until a person I trust tells me it's safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicky, but the office half of my job feels less certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you trust to tell you it's safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My team leader, Joanne, who's good at spotting what's useful. If she says use it, I'd use it. If she says wait, I'd wait with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that a risk, waiting for someone else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. You can be the last one to learn it and look slow, but I'd rather be second than first, because I've seen people jump on things that turned out useless.

say: I'd say it sounds big but I'd **wait and see** what it really does in a factory.
In the test bay I **can't see** software doing my work.
think: The drawings and checking half of my day could go, leaving **fewer engineers** and more technicians.
I'm slow with new technology and **I know it**.
do: Ask for more **test and commissioning work** and fewer drawing tasks.
Learn the new test-bay software when the company brings it in, with **Joanne's** say-so.
feel: **Uneasy**, not panicky; the office half of my job feels less certain.
S1.quote: You can be the last one to learn it and look slow, but I'd rather be second than first, because I've seen people jump on things that turned out useless.
fieldNote: He knows his **slow adoption** is a risk but is honest that he prefers it.
He trusts a specific person, his team leader Joanne, before any tool.
Say and think differ: publicly wait-and-see, privately a worry about the office half.

steps.text: Ask to do more test bay and commissioning work
Wait for Joanne's advice before trying any AI tool
Learn the company's new test software when it arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is crazy and no one is ready. I'd tell people at work that we should keep calm and ask the managers what the plan is. I wouldn't be posting online, I'm not like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be frightened. If AI can do almost any desk job, the office side of engineering is finished and the company doesn't need ten graduates. Robots for hands-on work take three more years, but a factory would be the first place to buy them, because the work is repetitive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending hard and save every pound for six months. I'd sell the car, because the loan isn't worth a car loan too, and move closer to the factory by renting a room in Derby. I'd put my name down for the apprentice-style technician work, because I'd rather have a job with my hands than none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a tight chest. I'd probably go quiet at home and not tell my parents how bad it feels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wouldn't you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad drives lorries and has his own worries about self-driving trucks, so I'd say everything's fine and not add mine. Then he'd put 200 in my account without asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that how you cope, by not saying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. I'd probably go and test pumps for a few hours and feel better, because the work makes sense even when the news doesn't.

say: I'd say two years is **crazy** and ask managers what the plan is.
I wouldn't post online; I'd **keep calm** at work.
think: If AI can do almost any desk job, the **office side** of engineering is finished.
A factory would be **first to buy robots** because the work repeats.
do: Sell the car and rent a room in **Derby** to cut costs.
Ask for **technician-style** hands-on work and save for six months.
feel: **Anxious**, with a tight chest, and I'd go quiet at home.
S2.quote: My dad drives lorries and has his own worries about self-driving trucks, so I'd say everything's fine and not add mine.
fieldNote: He **hides fear** from his parents, and the loss of the car is his first concrete cut.
His father's driving job gives him a second reason to worry about **robots**.
He plans for hands-on work because he cannot picture himself in AI work.

steps.text: Sell the car to stop the petrol and insurance costs
Save every spare pound towards six months of rent
Rent a room in Derby near the factory
Ask for a technician role working with my hands

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a bit of a warning, so let's see what they do about it. I'd tell the lads at the house to start putting something aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a bit more hopeful with five, because 2031 for the thinking side and 2034 for the hands-on side leaves me time. By 2031 I'll be 27, and I'd rather be a test engineer who runs rigs than someone behind a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for the test and commissioning side, get chartered, and save 300 a month. I'd learn the minimum to be safe with the new tools, probably after someone at work has already found the good ones. I'd also look at an apprenticeship-style route, like a service engineer role that travels to customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy but workable. Five years feels like a normal plan, not an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a service engineer do that a machine can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A service engineer turns up at a dairy at six in the morning and fixes the noisy pump with the right spanner. A robot might do that by 2034, but I'd say it's the last place it gets to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About seventy percent. The other thirty I keep to myself and lose a bit of sleep over.

say: I'd say five years is a **warning**, and my housemates should start saving.
I'd wait to see what **companies** do before saying more.
think: Five years feels hopeful, because by 2031 I'll be 27 and **running rigs** not sitting at a screen.
I believe the service-engineer idea about **seventy percent**.
do: Aim for test work, get **chartered**, and save 300 a month.
Look for a **service engineer** role that travels to customers.
feel: **Uneasy but workable**; five years feels like a plan, not an emergency.
S3.quote: A service engineer turns up at a dairy at six in the morning and fixes the noisy pump with the right spanner.
fieldNote: He gives himself a **seventy percent** belief in his own plan, an honest number.
His plan is tied to being physically present, which suits his **resistance to screens**.
Five years feels ordinary to him, not an emergency.

steps.text: Get chartered and move into test and commissioning work
Save 300 a month towards a safety cushion
Apply for a travelling service engineer role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for most things to be sorted out by sensible people. I'd tell myself not to panic yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be pretty calm. By 2036 I'll be 32 and probably a senior engineer on the shop floor, and the new tools will have been tested by a lot of people before they reach me. That suits the way I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, pass chartership, save for a house deposit with my girlfriend Beth, and slowly pick up the new tools when they're settled. I'd keep my feet in the test bay. And I'd pay down the loan so I'm not carrying it when something big happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the pace I like, slow enough to learn from other people's mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you even in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices. If everything gets cheaper because of AI that's fine, but if the money goes to a few big firms, the rest of us carry on paying rent. I'm not political, but that bit bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably vote, and make sure my mum has some savings. It's all I can do.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** for sensible people to sort it out.
I'd tell myself **not to panic** yet.
think: By 2036 I'll be 32 and a **senior engineer**, using tools that others tested first.
My worry is that gains go to a **few big firms**.
do: Pass **chartership** and save for a house deposit with my girlfriend Beth.
Pick up new tools once they're settled and pay down the **loan**.
feel: **Calm**; it's slow enough to learn from other people's mistakes.
S4.quote: If everything gets cheaper because of AI that's fine, but if the money goes to a few big firms, the rest of us carry on paying rent.
fieldNote: He is **calm** because the pace matches his style: others test the tools first.
His one worry, where the gains go, shows a **pragmatic centre** view rather than a party line.
He names a plan with Beth, the first mention of family-style plans.

steps.text: Pass chartership and stay in the test bay
Pay down the student loan faster
Save a house deposit with my girlfriend Beth
Vote for parties that share AI gains with workers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years, because I'd have no time to get my loan down and no idea what the company would do. What would help is a straight answer from the managers about what they plan, some savings, and a clear route into technician work for engineers who need it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. I'd just say I'm not a talker, so if I've sounded flat it's because I'd rather do than say.

headlineQuote: I'm not a talker, so if I've sounded flat it's because I'd rather do than say.
portrait: Zane is a 22-year-old **mechanical engineer** in his first job at a pump factory in Derby, owing about 19,000 on his degree.
He is resistant to new technology, **never uses AI tools**, and trusts older colleagues like Barry and his team leader Joanne.
His centre outlook shows in plain, practical answers and a wish that **gains are shared** without much politics.
He moves from relief at the plateau to a tight-chested **anxiety** at two years, steadier at five and calm at ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries him most, because he'd have no time to reduce his loan or learn what the firm plans.
whatWouldHelp: Straight answers from **managers**, some savings, and a clear route into technician work for engineers who need it.
